title: p99/p95 tail latency deep dive with Polaris Systems
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Polaris through p95/p99 tail latency analysis. Focus on streaming vs non-streaming, network hops, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed next steps: run a 1k request tail-latency benchmark with their 2048 token workload, share security docs, and schedule a dedicated pilot kick-off next week.
next_steps: Redwood to share latency benchmarking template + deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/latency-deep-dive.pdf
Polaris to provide sample workload and traffic profile (1k reqs, 2048 token avg)
Schedule pilot kickoff with Polaris infra + SecOps week of 2026-03-16
Redwood SE to run initial p95/p99 sims and share results by 2026-03-18
action_items: Miguel Santos - prepare benchmark harness and run 1k request test (due 2026-03-18)
Anika Rao - share sample prompts, token distributions, and SLO targets (due 2026-03-15)
Priya Menon - request security docs (SOC2, ISO) and confirm KMS plan (due 2026-03-16)

transcript:
Header: 2026-03-12 15:00 PDT | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Miguel Santos (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Polaris Head of ML), Tom Becker (Infra), Priya Menon (SecOps), Evan Liu (Product)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna focus on p95/p99 tail latency for the Polaris inference workload, and specifically look at streaming vs non-streaming and network hop effects. Miguel and I will share some numbers and recommendations.
[00:12] Anika Rao: Thanks Lena, excited — our main pain is occasional 5-10x spikes at the tail causing UI timeouts. Nominal qps is ~60 but bursts up to 200.
[00:25] Miguel Santos: Got it. Can you confirm your example workload? You mentioned 2k token max, average around 900-1k?
[00:34] Anika Rao: Yeah averages ~1k, but we have long multi-turn contexts hitting 2k sometimes. Also lots of streaming use for progressive responses.
[00:45] Tom Becker: We run in a VPC peered to Redwood dedicated, NAT in front, and typical cross-AZ hops. We suspect network jitter adding to tail too.
[00:58] Miguel Santos: Okay, quick outline: 1) p95 vs p99 differences come from both server-side scheduling (batching windows, preemption) and infra noise (network, GC, kernel scheduling), 2) Streaming reduces perceived latency but can increase CPU and kernel context switches, 3) KV cache hit ratio is crucial for long contexts.
[01:20] Priya Menon: On SecOps side we care about what telemetry we'll get — per-token latency traces, audit logs, and KMS flow. We'll need SOC2 docs.
[01:32] Lena Park: We'll share SOC2 and the security pack after the call — link in follow-up.
[01:38] Miguel Santos: Jumping into numbers — here's a slide we pasted in chat (link): https://redwood.ai/decks/latency-deep-dive.pdf. For a 1k token average non-streaming request on a loaded instance we typically see median ~120ms, p95 ~220ms, p99 ~380ms on our Dedicated profile for that model. These numbers vary with batch sizes and KV cache hit rate.
[02:08] Anika Rao: When you say "KV cache hit rate" how sensitive is p99 to that?
[02:12] Miguel Santos: Very; in our internal tests p99 can spike 2-4x if KV caches are cold. For long-context models, a miss forces recomputation of keys and increases per-token time. If you have prefix reuse across requests, even partial reuse gives big wins.
[02:30] Evan Liu: Is that warm by session, or per-worker? We use many short sessions from UI.
[02:36] Miguel Santos: Good question — KV cache is per-serving worker process. Short sessions with varied prefixes reduce hit rate; we recommend either sticky routing (session affinity) or prewarming common prefixes.
[02:50] Tom Becker: Sticky routing sounds hard with autoscale. Any recommended tradeoffs?
[02:55] Miguel Santos: You can do lightweight affinity for a subset of traffic, e.g., top 10% heavy sessions. Otherwise use aggressive prefix caching at the edge (client side) or reduce batch windows to favor low latency.
[03:08] [03:10] Lena Park: Let's talk streaming — Miguel?
[03:12] Miguel Santos: Streaming yields first-byte latency improvement because you send tokens as they are decoded. For p95 perceived latency (time-to-first-token) streaming often beats non-streaming, but p99 for overall request completion can still be dominated by last token generation and network retries. Also, streaming keeps connections open longer which interacts with TCP slow start and ephemeral port exhaustion in high-concurrency setups.
[03:40] Anika Rao: We saw timeouts when connections were held for streaming during peaks. So is non-streaming safer?
[03:46] Miguel Santos: Not necessarily. Non-streaming batches can increase queuing delay — e.g., batching window of 20-50ms improves throughput but hurts p95 if traffic is sparse. Streaming gives earlier visible progress but requires more headroom in connection counts and tuning of keepalives.
[04:03] Priya Menon: About network hops — Tom mentioned cross-AZ. How much does a single extra hop add?
[04:10] Miguel Santos: Rough heuristic: cross-AZ adds 1-2ms median but tail effects can be amplified by 10-50ms depending on router jitter. Also if you're going through NAT + firewall + proxy, each adds queuing. For p99 these add up. We saw a customer where removing a double NAT cut p99 by ~80ms.
[04:30] Tom Becker: Ours currently does NAT -> firewall -> load balancer -> Redwood. Should we try direct VPC peering?
[04:36] Miguel Santos: Yes, VPC peering or PrivateLink reduces hops and jitter. For private deployments (on-prem) you also control path — but then you must manage GPU utilization and batch configuration yourself.
[04:50] Anika Rao: On quantization — we are evaluating int8 to cut cost. How does quant affect tail latency?
[04:56] Miguel Santos: Int8 often reduces per-token latency (and memory bandwidth), but worst-case latency can increase if kernels fall back or dequant/quantize steps are added for certain ops. Our runtime has optimized int8 kernels; when properly matched to the model we usually see ~10-25% lower median and p95, but p99 improvements depend on kernel stability under high concurrency. There are edge cases where int8 triggers slower paths for attention because of precision compensation.
[05:24] Evan Liu: So we should test int8 under load.
[05:26] Miguel Santos: Exactly — we recommend A/B on the same shape of workload, and watch p99 specifically. Also watch for subtle quality regressions; Redwood Optimize can help pick quant profiles.
[05:38] [06:00] Lena Park: Let's surface a concrete checklist for Polaris. Miguel, can you describe benchmark harness?
[06:05] Miguel Santos: Sure — we'll run 1k request runs with your token distribution. We'll do 3 passes: cold KV cache, warm KV cache (after prewarming), and streaming vs non-streaming. We'll capture per-token timings, network RTT from client to server, worker scheduling delays, and batch sizes. We'll also simulate spikes (burst to 200 qps). Results include median, p95, p99, and the CDF.
[06:34] Anika Rao: For cold vs warm — how long to prewarm?
[06:37] Miguel Santos: A short prewarm (100-200 representative requests) often suffices to approximate steady-state prefix cache. We'll document heuristics.
[06:44] Tom Becker: About batching windows — what's your recommendation for 60 qps baseline?
[06:49] Miguel Santos: If traffic is stable at 60 qps, small batching window (10-20ms) gives good throughput with limited p95 impact. For bursty loads, shorter windows or adaptive batching (reduce window when queue length small) is better. You can set a max tokens per batch too.
[07:05] Priya Menon: One of our constraints is that SecOps requires audit logs for every request and encryption with our KMS. Does that add tail latency?
[07:13] Miguel Santos: KMS calls on every request would add network round trips if you do a per-request remote KMS. Typical pattern is envelope encryption where the model keys are cached in a secure HSM or local KMS agent — so per-request overhead is small. We support customer-managed keys with a handshake that happens once per worker start. We'll include implementation notes in the security pack.
[07:34] Anika Rao: You mentioned adaptive batching — does Redwood runtime automatically change batch sizes?
[07:38] Miguel Santos: Yes, our serving runtime has adaptive batching policies that adjust window and batch size based on p99 latency SLO and current queue length. You can provide a target p99 and it will try to meet it by lowering the batching window or spilling to extra workers.
[07:54] Evan Liu: Are there tradeoffs with autoscaling? Sometimes scale-up is slow and increases p99 while new workers warm caches.
[07:59] Miguel Santos: Correct — scale events cause cold caches and increased p99. To mitigate: pre-provision buffer capacity, warm new workers with common prefixes, or route traffic so heavy sessions stay on warm workers. For Dedicated we offer burst capacity to handle that.
[08:15] [08:20] Tom Becker: Any quick wins we can do in our infra?
[08:22] Miguel Santos: Yes — reduce NAT/filter hops, move to VPC peering, increase TCP keepalive to avoid connection churn, reduce batching window during spikes, and consider a small sticky routing layer for heavy sessions. Also add per-request tracing to correlate network latency vs server latency.
[08:40] Anika Rao: Can Redwood provide per-token traces?
[08:42] Miguel Santos: Yes — we can instrument per-token timings and provide a trace view in the Console and CSV export. We'll include sample traces in the benchmark results.
[08:52] [09:05] Priya Menon: On compliance — can you confirm retention and where logs live for Dedicated vs Private?
[09:10] Lena Park: For Dedicated redwood-managed, logs are stored in our audit cluster with configurable retention; for Private you control storage. We'll send the security doc.
[09:20] Anika Rao: Ok, a slightly nitty question — what about Linux CFS scheduling or kernel parameters you tune? We run K8s nodes with mixed workloads.
[09:29] Miguel Santos: Kernel and CPU isolation matter. We recommend node pinning for serving workers, CPU isolcpus flags for real-time cores, and avoiding noisy neighbors on the same GPU hosts. On K8s we recommend exclusive node pools for inference and use RT kernel tweaks where allowed. We'll share our ops notes.
[09:48] Evan Liu: Regarding monitoring — what dashboards should we watch first?
[09:51] Miguel Santos: p99 latency, batch size distribution, KV cache hit rate, worker GC/CPU stalls, and network RTTs. Also track connection counts for streaming. Redwood Console provides these out-of-the-box, plus flamegraphs for hotspots.
[10:05] [10:30] Lena Park: We're running a little over time but this has been great. Quick recap and owners?
[10:36] Miguel Santos: Recap: Run 1k request benchmark (cold/warm/streaming), test int8 under load, evaluate VPC peering to reduce hops, and share security/compliance docs.
[10:46] Anika Rao: Sounds good. We want the benchmark results and policy recommendations before the pilot kickoff.
[10:50] Lena Park: We'll get the harness and run the first pass; Miguel will deliver the results. I'll send pricing and the security pack after the call.
[11:00] [11:20] Tom Becker: One last Q — if we do on-prem private deployment, how different will p99 be?
[11:25] Miguel Santos: On-prem removes network jitter and hops so network-contributed tail drops, but you take on ops variability. If you match GPU types and kernel builds, on-prem p99 can be equal or better. Biggest risk is scale — cluster autoscaling and cache warm-up management become your responsibility.
[11:42] Anika Rao: Great. Let's schedule pilot kickoff 2026-03-17 10am PT.
[11:48] Lena Park: I'll propose that slot. Thanks everyone.
[11:52] [END] Note: transcript contains some ASR artifacts — e.g., "K V cache" instead of "KV cache" and occasional speaker labeling inconsistencies.
